blocks.content: Puducherry's culture chapter is dominated by its unique Franco-Tamil colonial heritage and by Auroville — an internationally significant experimental township that draws heavy and specific exam attention in its own right.

Puducherry town's historic core is divided into the 'White Town' (Ville Blanche) — the former French administrative and residential quarter, featuring grid-planned streets, colonial-era villas with distinctive yellow-washed walls, bougainvillea-draped courtyards, and French street names — and the 'Black Town' (Ville Noire), the traditional Tamil quarter, separated historically by the Grand Canal (Chapter 1).

This heritage quarter has been actively preserved and promoted as a tourism and architectural-conservation asset, with INTACH (Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage) and other conservation bodies involved in heritage-building preservation efforts; the French Quarter's distinctive character continues to draw comparisons with Goa's own, separately distinct Indo-Portuguese heritage architecture.

The Puducherry Museum, the French War Memorial (on the town's seafront promenade, commemorating French Indian soldiers who died in the First World War), and the Sri Aurobindo Ashram (below) are among the town's other major heritage landmarks.

★ EXAM POINT: Puducherry's Franco-Tamil 'White Town/Black Town' urban heritage is conceptually and architecturally distinct from Goa's Indo-Portuguese heritage and from Daman/Diu's Indo-Portuguese forts (covered in the companion DNH&DD GS volume) — each reflects a DIFFERENT European colonial power's distinct architectural and urban-planning tradition.

The Sri Aurobindo Ashram, founded in Puducherry in 1926 by the philosopher-yogi Sri Aurobindo (a former Indian nationalist revolutionary who later turned to spiritual pursuits) and 'The Mother' (Mirra Alfassa, a French-born spiritual collaborator), is one of India's most internationally recognised spiritual/philosophical institutions, drawing devotees, scholars and visitors from across India and abroad.

Sri Aurobindo's own philosophical and spiritual writings (including 'The Life Divine' and his concept of 'Integral Yoga') and The Mother's subsequent leadership of the Ashram after Aurobindo's death in 1950 shaped the institution's distinctive spiritual-philosophical identity, which later directly inspired the founding of Auroville (below).

★ EXAM POINT: Sri Aurobindo Ashram (founded 1926) and Auroville (founded 1968, below) are related but DISTINCT institutions — the Ashram is the older, foundational spiritual institution; Auroville is a later, separate international township directly INSPIRED by the Ashram's philosophy and founded by The Mother.

Auroville ('City of Dawn') is an experimental international township founded on 28 February 1968 by The Mother (Mirra Alfassa), envisioned as a universal, planned community 'belonging to no nation' dedicated to human unity and sustainable living, situated partly within Puducherry's territory and partly within neighbouring Tamil Nadu (Villupuram district) — making it another distinctive cross-boundary geographic feature associated with the UT.

Auroville's inauguration ceremony was attended by representatives of 124 countries and all Indian states, who symbolically contributed soil from their home regions to a central urn — a foundational ritual still commemorated in Auroville's institutional identity today.

The township's most iconic architectural feature is the Matrimandir ('Temple of the Mother'), a large golden-spheroid meditation structure at Auroville's geographical and spiritual centre, designed by architect Roger Anger and completed (in its main structural form) in 2008 after decades of construction, now one of Puducherry's most visited landmarks.

Auroville operates under a distinctive administrative and legal framework of its own, governed by the Auroville Foundation, established under the Auroville Foundation Act, 1988 (a central Act of Parliament), reflecting Auroville's unique status as neither a conventional municipality nor a purely private township, but a specially constituted foundation with its own governing board, international advisory council and residents' assembly.

Partly in Puducherry UT, partly in Tamil Nadu (Villupuram district) — a cross-boundary township

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Auroville's governing legal instrument is a specific ACT OF PARLIAMENT (the Auroville Foundation Act, 1988) — not merely a state/UT regulation — reflecting its unique national and international significance; this is a frequently tested administrative-law fact distinguishing Auroville from an ordinary municipality or private trust.

items: Pongal (the Tamil harvest festival) and other major Tamil festivals are widely celebrated across the Tamil-speaking regions (Puducherry, Karaikal), reflecting the UT's predominant Tamil cultural character.

Bastille Day (14 July, the French National Day) continues to be marked with some ceremonial observance in Puducherry, a distinctive legacy of the region's French colonial history, alongside Indian national festivals and observances.
The Puducherry Heritage Festival and various government-promoted cultural events showcase the UT's blended Franco-Tamil identity as part of broader tourism promotion (Chapter 11).
Puducherry town's 'White Town' (French quarter) and 'Black Town' (Tamil quarter) are divided by the historic Grand Canal.
Sri Aurobindo Ashram founded 1926 by Sri Aurobindo and The Mother (Mirra Alfassa).
Auroville ('City of Dawn') founded 28 February 1968 by The Mother; spans both Puducherry UT and Tamil Nadu; Matrimandir is its iconic structure.
Auroville is governed by the Auroville Foundation under the Auroville Foundation Act, 1988 (a Parliamentary Act).
Bastille Day (14 July) continues to be observed in Puducherry, reflecting its French colonial heritage.
